subsections.title: Government
subsections.content:
- Type:  Presidential -parliamentary democracy with a multi -party system. The

President is directly elected for up to two consecutive five -year terms, while the Prime Minister, who holds most executive powers, is appointed by the President based on legislative elec tion results.

- Stability:  Governments are often short -lived due to proportional

representation, which encourages coalition or minority governments.

- Civil Liberties:  Civil liberties are generally respected, though poverty and

corruption weaken some institutions and reduce judicial efficiency.

- Judicial Independence:  The judiciary is partially independent but susceptible

to political influence and corruption. A three -year judicial modernization program was launched in 2020 to enhance judicial and prosecutorial independence. principe/freedom -world/2021

subsections.title: Trade (Political Context)
subsections.content:
- São Tomé and Príncipe has a weakly integrated trade system , as it is not yet

a member of the WTO. Although it applied for accession in 2005, the process remains stalled, limiting alignment with global trade standards and reducing international trade credibility. cipe_e.htm?utm_source=chatgpt.com

- Trade is highly concentrated geographically , with exports mainly directed to

European countries (e.g., Netherlands, Belgium, Portugal, Germany, and Spain), while imports are dominated by Portugal and a few African and international partners (e.g., Togo, Angola, Japan, and Turkey). LTST/TradeFlow/Import/Partner/all Trade  structure: The country exhibits a significant trade imbalance, with imports (≈ $165 million in 2024) far exceeding exports, which remain very limited and narrow in scope

- The export base is undiversified, relying primarily on cocoa and low -value

materials, while imports consist mainly of food, manufactured goods, and essential commodities  indicating  strong dependence on external markets . 2025

- Trade policies  remain relatively flexible , with moderate tariff levels (~10%),

but the absence of WTO membership results  in a lack of binding commitments and weaker positioning in global trade negotiations.

- Overall trade volume is very small on a global scale , as reflected by minimal

trade relations with major economies (e.g., total trade with the United States ≈ $1.6 million in 2024).

subsections.title: Tax Policies (Political / Fiscal Context)
subsections.content:
- São Tomé and Príncipe operates a developing tax system with limited

administrative capacity and enforcement challenges.

- São Tomé and Príncipe operates a structured tax system under the Ministry of

Economy and Finance, with progressive personal income tax rates reaching up to 25% and social security contributions totaling 14% (8% employer and 6% employee).

- The government introduced a Value Added Tax (VAT) at a standard rate of 10%

to modernize the tax system and improve revenue collection in line with international recommendations.

- The fiscal framework also includes withholding taxes on dividends (10 –15%),

interest (10%), royalties (10%), and technical service fees (15%), indicating a relatively defined and organized tax structure.

- The tax system incorporates multiple regimes (general and simplified) and

provides incentives such as tax exemptions, reduced import duties, and deductions to support investment and small businesses.

- However, the effectiveness of tax policies is limited by weak administrative

capacity, tax evasion, and a large informal sector, resulting in low revenue efficiency and continued reliance on indirect taxation and external financial support. https://www.globalexpansion.com/hubfs/Countrypedia%20PDFs/In%20use/S ao%20Tome%20and%20Principe%20 -%20Global%20Employer%20Guide.pdf https://www.britacom.org/zt/ThemeDay/Tenth/SEMINAR/202510/P0202510 21566751498936.pdf

subsections.title: General political issues
subsections.content:
São Tomé and Príncipe faces several governance and institutional challenges despite maintaining a generally democratic system. Key concerns include limited government accountability , as reflected in reported cases of police abuse and delayed or incomplete investigations into misconduct.

- Freedom of expression is constitutionally guaranteed and generally respected;

however, media independence is constrained by political influence, self - censorship, and limited access to official information , particularly in state - owned media.

- The country experiences weak transparency and information accessibility ,

with journalists reporting difficulties in obtaining official data and concerns over biased media coverage favoring the ruling coalition.

- Although labor laws formally guarantee rights such as unionization and

collective bargaining, enforcement remains weak , with limited inspections, lack of penalties, and ineffective protection against labor violations.

- A significant structural issue is the large informal sector (estimated at around

68% of the workforce) , which undermines regulatory effectiveness, tax collection, and overall economic governance.

- More broadly, institutional capacity constraints , including limited human

resources, weak enforcement mechanisms, and insufficient regulatory oversight, continue to affect policy implementation and governance efficiency. rights -practices/sao -tome -and-principe  2024

subsections.title: Change in Leadership
subsections.content:
- São Tomé and Príncipe transitioned from a one -party state (1975 –1991) to a

multi -party democracy with multiple peaceful power transfers.

- Key recent changes: 2016 presidential election dispute; 2018 legislative

elections led to coalition government formation; 2020 legislation prevented citizens born abroad from running for president, targeting ADI party leader Patrice Trovoada.

subsections.title: Regulations
subsections.content:
- Electoral Laws: Generally fair, though implementation suffers from limited

resources and staff.

- Legislative Actions: National Assembly enacts laws affecting elections and

governance, such as restricting presidential candidacy for citizens born abroad and appointing election commissioners.

- Government Transparency: Access to information is partially available; no

specific law guarantees full transparency.

- Judiciary: Laws provide judicial independence, but political influence and

corruption remain concerns.

subsections.title: Political Trends
subsections.content:
- Multiparty Competition: Free and vigorous competition among ADI, MLSTP -

PSD, PCD -UDD -MDFM, and other parties, despite occasional factional splits.

- Democratic Stability: Multiple peaceful democratic transitions demonstrate

resilience, with real opportunities for opposition parties.

- Civil Society: NGOs, including human rights and governance organizations,

operate freely, though underfunded. Challenges:  Corruption, weak institutions, societal discrimination against women and LGBT+ groups, and limited enforcement capacity for social and economic regulations. world/2023

subsections.title: Inflation
subsections.content:
São Tomé and Príncipe experiences relatively high but declining inflation, reaching approximately 9.5% in January 2026 , down from 10.3% in December 2025, marking the lowest level since early 2022.

- Despite recent improvements, inflation remains elevated compared to global

averages, reflecting ongoing cost -of-living pressures.

- Historically, inflation has been high and volatile , averaging around 14.5% since

1997 , with extreme fluctuations ranging from a peak of 86.8% to lows near 3.5%, indicating structural instability in price levels.

- In Sao Tome and Principe, the main components of the Consumer Price Index

are: Food & Non -alcoholic Beverages (73% of the total weight), Housing & Utilities (6%) and Transport (4%). Household Contents, Equipment & Maintenance accounts for 4%, Alcoholic Bev erages & Tobacco for 4%, and Clothing & Footwear for 3%. Others include: Communications (2%), Restaurants & Hotels (2%), Miscellaneous Goods & Services (2%), Recreation & Culture (1%), Education (0.44%), and Health (0.41%). Overall, while inflation is sho wing signs of stabilization, it continues to pose a key economic challenge affecting purchasing power and economic stability.

subsections.title: Interest rate
subsections.content:
- The benchmark interest rate in São Tomé and Príncipe is approximately 10% ,

reflecting a relatively high cost of borrowing in the economy.

- Historically, interest rates have remained elevated, averaging around 14.3%

since 1998 , with significant volatility ranging from a peak of 29.5% to a low of 9%, indicating periods of monetary instability.

- The relatively high interest rate is primarily used as a tool to control inflation ,

which has been persistently high in the country.

- However, elevated borrowing costs may limit private investment and

economic expansion , particularly in a small and developing economy. rate

subsections.title: Exchange rate
subsections.content:
- The São Tomé and Príncipe dobra (STN) is relatively weak, with an exchange

rate of approximately 21.4 STN per USD (March 2026) .

- In the short term, the currency has shown slight depreciation (around 2.3%

over the past month) , indicating ongoing pressure on the local currency.

- However, over the past year, the dobra has appreciated by approximately

6.5% , suggesting a degree of medium -term stabilization.

- The exchange rate is supported by a currency peg to the euro , which helps

maintain stability and control inflation but increases dependence on external reserves and limits monetary policy flexibility.

- Overall, while the exchange rate shows relative stability, it remains

vulnerable to external shocks and foreign exchange constraints. 2026

subsections.title: Economic Growth
subsections.content:
- São Tomé and Príncipe recorded modest economic growth of approximately

1.7% in 2024 , reflecting a slight recovery from 0.5% in 2023, but remaining below its historical average of around 4.1%.

- The economy is very small , with a GDP of approximatley $0.76 billion  and low

income levels (GDP per capita ≈ $1,365), highlighting its developing status.

- Economic activity is largely concentrated in agriculture (especially cocoa) and

tourism , with declining cocoa production due to droughts and mismanagement affecting overall growth performance.

- The country is increasingly dependent on foreign aid  and highly vulnerable to

external shocks, particularly fluctuations in global food and fuel prices.

- Political instability remains a potential risk that could negatively impact

economic growth and foreign direct investment.

- However, the discovery of oil reserves in the Gulf of Guinea  presents a

potential long -term opportunity to boost economic growth, if successfully developed. annual

subsections.title: Unemployment rate
subsections.content:
- Unemployment in São Tomé and Príncipe remains relatively stable, averaging

around 9–10% between 2020 and 2025 , with only slight fluctuations over time.

- While there was a modest decline from approximately 9.7% in 2020 to around

9.0% in 2022, unemployment levels have since remained largely unchanged, indicating limited job creation.

- A key structural challenge is the large informal sector (estimated at around

68% of the workforce) , which distorts official unemployment figures and reflects widespread underemployment and job insecurity.

- As a result, the labor market is characterized by low productivity, weak job

quality, and limited formal employment opportunities , despite relatively stable unemployment rates. https://data.worldbank.org/indicator/SL.UEM.TOTL.ZS?end=2025&locations=ST&sta rt=2020&view=chart  2025

- Population growth:

São Tomé and Príncipe's population is growing steadily at about 2.0 -2.1% annually, reaching around 247,000 in 2026 from 242,000 in 2025. Growth Drivers

- High fertility rates (around 3.95 children per woman) and a youthful

demographic fuel natural increase of about 5,000 people yearly, outpacing net migration losses of roughly 900.

- This continues a decades -long trend from 2.0% in the 1990s to peaks near

2.7% in the 1970s, with density rising to 258 people per km².

subsections.title: culture lifestyle attitudes
subsections.content:
- São Tomé and Príncipe residents embrace a relaxed "Leve Leve" lifestyle,

emphasizing simplicity, community harmony, and resilience shaped by their island paradise and Luso -African heritage . ### 2.3.3.1 — Core Values

- People prioritize elder respect, social unity, and strength in adversity, rooted

in colonial and slavery histories that fostered mutual support . Peaceful coexistence prevails in a mestizo society blending Portuguese, African, and creole influences, with Christianity dominant but coexisting with traditional practices. subsections.title: 2 Daily Attitudes
subsections.content:
- A laid -back approach —"go slowly" —defines routines, with strong family

bonds, communal living in rural areas, and growing gender equality in modern sectors.

- Lifestyle revolves around fresh seafood, tropical fruits, music/dance like

tchiloli, and festivals celebrating independence or saints, reflecting optimism and cultural pride The Culture Of Sao Tome And Principe

subsections.title: Educational levels
subsections.content:
- Educational Outcomes and Human Capital

- In 2024, São Tomé and Príncipe, like many other African countries, is facing a

learning crisis. In sub -Saharan Africa, learning poverty, defined as the share of children unable to read and understand an age -appropriate text by age 10, is estimated  at 89 percent  by the World Bank,

- In 2023, São Tomé and Príncipe has made strides in education, with primary

enrollment near 98% and adult literacy at 93%, but challenges persist in completion rates and quality. ### 2.3.4.1 — Literacy and Access

- Adult literacy rose from 74.9% a decade ago to 93% by 2023, driven by the

Quality Education for All Project since 2014, which boosted teacher training and infrastructure.

- Youth (15 -24) literacy nears universality, though 2% have no formal

education and 36% incomplete primary, per older EPDC data. ### 2.3.4.2 — Enrollment Breakdown

- Primary completion stands at 87%, with 96% net enrollment, but secondary

transition dips below 60% and completion lower, especially in rural areas.

- The 6 -3-3 system sees high primary access but dropouts due to poverty;

higher education remains limited, aligning with Vision 2030 human capital goals. Sao Tomeans segment their education into pre -primary, primary, secondary and tertiary levels, and while education is legally mandated for children between 6 and 14 years old, many children, particularly young girls, face challenges in attending school. Oft en, people encourage them to stay home and learn the traditional role of women rather than skills to join the workforce. subsections.title: Buying habits
subsections.content:
- São Tomé and Príncipe residents prioritize essential goods amid economic

pressures, with household consumption dominating at 81.4% of GDP and heavy reliance on imported food, fuel, and staples. Spending Priorities

- High inflation (peaking above 20% recently) squeezes purchasing power,

driving focus on necessities like rice, fish, vegetables, and price -controlled basics, with government exemptions aiding affordability.

- Limited disposable income (GDP per capita ~$2,400) favors informal markets,

local produce, and subsistence in rural areas, while urban households allocate more to utilities and remittances.  Consumption Patterns

- Imports dwarf exports (35% vs. 3.6% of GDP), reflecting import -dependent

habits for consumer goods, with low savings and debt distress curbing luxury or durable purchases.

- Emerging tourism boosts demand for services, but inequality (Gini 40.7)

means poorer 44.6% live near poverty lines, emphasizing value -for-money and community sharing. CDP-PL-2025 -STP.pdf São Tomé and Príncipe - STP

Argel Accord Day. Prior to the nation being granted independence, the Argel Accords

- São Tomé has a large Christian population, accounting for about 80 percent

subsections.title: Health and Healthcare System
subsections.content:
### 2.3.9.1 — What is healthcare in Sao Tome and Principe like? Health consciousness:

- São Tomé and Príncipe shows mixed health consciousness, with rising

awareness of some risks but persistent unhealthy behaviors amid NCD program efforts. Key Trends (2008 -2019)

- Overweight/obesity climbed to 51%, especially among women (58.1%),

signaling low focus on diet control despite better fruit/vegetable intake (down to 53.3%).

- Physical inactivity doubled to 30.9%, with women more affected, while

tobacco use (8.8%) and hypertension (33.5%) stayed stable.

- Positive shifts include reduced frequent alcohol (24.8%) and diabetes (1.2%),

more among men, tied to partial NCD integration in primary care. Awareness Factors

- Higher education links to less alcohol and poor diets but more obesity,

suggesting nutrition knowledge gaps in urban/educated groups.

- Limited campaigns on activity, tobacco, and diet hinder progress, per WHO

reports, despite STEPS surveys boosting data -driven interventions. What about the medical facilities?

- Medical facilities in São Tomé and Príncipe are extremely limited. There is

one hospital in the country on the island of São Tomé, Hospital Central Ayres de Menezes, phone number 239 2 -221-222. A few clinics also exist, but the service provided is very bas ic. For all but minor medical needs, it is necessary to travel to Libreville (Gabon), Lisbon (Portugal), or elsewhere. You should carry an ample supply of properly labeled prescription drugs and other medications with you; an adequate supply of prescriptio n or over -the- counter drugs in local stores or pharmacies is generally not available.

- Tap water may not be potable and you should drink and cook with bottled

water only. Schistosomiasis, also known as bilharzia, is endemic to São Tomé and Príncipe. Schistosomiasisis a parasite that can penetrate intact skin of those swimming or bathing in f resh water from lakes, rivers and streams. It is recommended to avoid contact with untreated fresh water to prevent schistosomiasis infection. https://www.countryreports.org/country/SaoTomeandPrincipe/health.htm Frontiers | Trends in bio -behavioural risk factors of non -communicable diseases among adults in Sao Tome and Principe ### 2.3.9.2 — The Four Most Common Diseases in Sao Tome and Principe: 1. Tuberculosis (TB) is a bacterial disease easily communicable in the first few weeks of visible symptoms. 2. Malaria, spread through mosquitoes, is an endemic for most impoverished African countries, including Sao Tome Principe. 3. Cholera is actively transmitted in many impoverished countries, including Sao Tome and Principe. 4. Necrotizing cellulitis is a rare disease, but an outbreak earlier this year has left Sao Tome and Principe vulnerable. Note:  More than 1,300 cases of necrotizing cellulitis, a  severe skin infection  known for intense pain and swollen tissues, have been reported since September 2016. To date, every health district in the country has reported cases, and the country’s 190,000 inhabitants are at risk. Cases have been increasing but no deaths directly linked to the disease have been recorded. ### 2.3.9.3 — Healthcare Infrastructure in São Tomé and Príncipe 1.Hospital Central de São Tomé (São Tomé Central Hospital)

subsections.title: Transportation and Daily Life
subsections.content:
Taxis and Car Rental

- Car rentals are available in the country and there are a few international

companies that have a presence but the more popular options are often through local companies, which are cheaper and offer equally reliable services. The network of roads in the cou ntry is extensive, adding up to about 230 miles. That said, most of the roads are in poor condition and several are unpaved. If travelers are intent on renting a vehicle, they should consider a four -wheel drive, which is far better equipped to deal with th e unpredictable nature of many routes in the country.

- There are a few private taxi services in the country, mainly operating the

route between São Tomé International Airport and the city center. There are also shared taxis in most of the cities, which are identifiable by their bright yellow color and can simp ly be flagged down at the side of the road. Journeys within cities have fixed prices and travelers simply need to pass the money to the front of the taxi at some point during the journey. The prices of journeys outside of the city need to be negotiated bef orehand. Trains and Buses

- São Tomé once had a thriving railway system but this network has since been

abandoned. Today, there are no rail services in the country and while sightseeing, travelers may even stumble upon the ruins of a few old railway stations and abandoned carriages.

- There are no private bus companies or coach services in the country. The

only way to navigate between regions is to take a minibus taxi, which can be flagged down in cities or found waiting at communal taxi ranks. The fares for long distance trips should b e agreed upon prior to departure as there are no set routes. Travelers who wish to navigate their way between islands can do so either by ferry or local airline. principe/transportation Renting a Car in Sao Tome Island with No Security Deposit

- When you pick up the car, you'll often be required to leave a deposit on your

credit card or debit card. Deposits vary significantly subject to the size of the vehicle and the excess amount. Car rental Security deposits in Sao Tome Island can be anywhere b etween £100 and £2,500. and-principe/sao -tome -island

subsections.title: Current Situation of Existing Inequalities in São Tomé and Príncipe
subsections.content: Post-Independence Evolution (1975 -Present) - After independence in 1975, São Tomé and Príncipe struggled to address historical inequalities. The Forros, composed of approximately 50% of the population, continued to dominate political and economic life, while the serviçais (30%) and Angolares (10%) re mained marginalized. Economic Disparities: The 2021 Annual Report by the Central Bank of São Tomé and Príncipe noted high poverty rates, with about half the population living below the poverty line, particularly in rural areas. The decline of cocoa production exacerbated economic challenges, leavin g rural communities —primarily comprised of serviçais and Angolares —with limited access to infrastructure and economic opportunities. Urban areas, where Forros are more concentrated, enjoy better access to services and higher income levels, as highlighted i n a 2012 study by the São Tomé and Príncipe Institute for Social and Economic Research (INEP), which showed educational and income disparities between forros and other groups. Ethnic and Social Inequalities: Cultural values among the Forro population, such as clientelism and corruption, have been cited as persistent obstacles to development. Serviçais, descendants of contract laborers, often work in informal economies as "candongueiros" (informal traders), whi le Angolares, primarily involved in fishing, continue to face challenges due to their geographic isolation in southern areas like São João dos Angolares. The land reforms of the 1990s, supported by the World Bank, aimed to redistribute land to ex -serviçais  but did not entirely alleviate socioeconomic disparities, particularly for rural ex -serviçais and Angolares. Urban -Rural Divide: A significant urban -rural divide exists in the country, with about 60% of the population living in urban areas that have better access to education, healthcare, and economic opportunities. Rural populations, disproportionately comprising serviçais and Ango lares, suffer from higher poverty rates, with a 2020 poverty headcount ratio at $1.90 a day (2011 PPP) standing at 35.6%. This divide is exacerbated by the vulnerability of rural agricultural communities to external shocks, including climate change. Gender and Regional Disparities: A 2019 UNDP report highlights gender inequalities, noting that women in São Tomé and Príncipe have lower literacy rates and limited access to economic opportunities. Regional disparities also persist, particularly with Príncipe being less developed than São Tomé. Rural women, often from serviçais or Angolares backgrounds, face compounded disadvantages due to these intersecting factors.

subsections.title: Level of Technology at schools

the World Bank, many schools have limited access to computers and internet, and teachers often lack digital training. At the university level, institutions such as the University of São Tomé and Príncipe offer technology -related courses , helping students gain digital skills. Overall, technology in education is growing but still faces challenges like infrastructure and access.

subsections.title: Summary
subsections.content:
- The Country of Sao Tome and Principe has undergone a TNA ( Technology

Needs Assessment) that was completed by the end of 2023 to Identify what   kind of technologies are best suited to a country’s specific climate change situation and   assess and analyse the  country’s specific needs, as relates to its specific set of circumstances and utilize this data to set priorities and identify appropriate technologies.

- The Main Findings and Conclusions of the study can be summarized in the

following points:

- Focus sectors: Energy  and Transport , chosen for their high emissions and

strategic importance.

- São Tomé and Príncipe remains a net carbon sink but faces rising emissions in

energy and transport.

- Prioritized technologies will guide future mitigation projects and support the

transition to a low-carbon, climate -resilient economy . The chosen sectors for adaptation were agroforestry and water, and for mitigation, energy and transport. The corresponding prioritised technologies for these sectors were:

- Agroforestry: protected cultivation integrated in greenhouses, sustainable

agricultural land management, agro -silvo -pastoral system

- Water: integrated management of hydrographic basins, water safety plan,

construction and maintenance of existing dams and water reservoirs

- Energy: solar photovoltaic power plant, hydroelectric power, efficient

management of the electricity system

- Transport: electric light cars, electric motorcycles, electric public transport

with photovoltaic roofs in Enviromental too)

subsections.title: Overview
subsections.content:
- São Tomé and Príncipe is the second smallest country in Africa and is a Small

Island Developing State. The country faces significant challenges in the face of climate change including land degradation caused by commercial logging, unsustainable agriculture  and competing demands for food, energy, and space, and increasing ocean acidification, coastal floods, and marine degradation

- The NDC identified the most vulnerable sectors as agriculture, fisheries, and

livestock. Horticultural and vegetable production are highly exposed to extreme weather events, such as floods, droughts, and heavy rains.

- These crops are drastically affected by pests, requiring substantial agricultural

inputs and agrochemicals, which increases land -based waste that ends up in groundwater layers and the sea.

- The country consists of an archipelago with two main islands, São Tomé Island

which is 50 km long and 30 km wide, and Príncipe Island which is about 30 km long and 6 km wide. The coastal zone includes the slopes of extinct volcanoes, within which the envir onment is under stress from soil degradation and coastal erosion. A Multi -Sector Investment Plan (MSIP)  was developed for the country which emphasized the need for policy reforms that promote more sustainable and adaptive management of the coastal zones, a new institutional framework for disaster risk management, and a strong community engagement for coastal  protection. Multi -Sector Investment Plan (MSIP)

subsections.title: WACA Interventions
subsections.content:
- Ongoing activities focus on natural -based solutions through community

approaches and hybrid solutions, when hard solutions are indispensable, beach nourishment, drainage, breakwaters, and coastal and riverbank revetments. On policy interventions, a new law on sand extraction is being supported. Community -based adaptation is a center of the approach in Sao Tome and Principe, including support to schemes for routine maintenance of coastal protection infrastructure in collaboration with district governments. Key agencies

- The Ministry of Infrastructure, Natural Resources and Environment is the lead

agency for coastal resilience efforts. It has established a project implementation unit to coordinate project activities supported by multiple partners.

subsections.title: Geography
subsections.content:
- Location : Western Africa; islands straddling the equator in the Gulf of Guinea

west of Gabon.

- Area : 1,001 sq. km. (386 sq. mi.); about the size of metropolitan Indianapolis, or

one-third the size of Rhode Island.

- Cities : Capital --Sao Tome.  Other cities --Trinidade, Santana, Angolares, Neves,

Santo Antonio.

- Terrain : Two small, volcanic islands.

- Climate : Tropical, with wet and dry seasons, influenced by the mountainous

topography. The islands of Sao Tome and Principe, situated in the equatorial Atlantic about 300 and 250 kilometres (200 mi. and 150 mi.), respectively, off the northwest coast of Gabon, constitute Africa's smallest country. Both are part of an extinct volcanic mountai n range, which also includes the island of Bioko in Equatorial Guinea to the north and Mount Cameroon on the African west coast. Sao Tome is 50 kilometres (31 mi.) long and 32 kilometres (20 mi.) wide and the more mountainous of the two islands. Its peaks reach 2,024 meters (6,640 ft.). Principe is about 30 kilometres (19 mi.) long and 6 kilometres (4 mi.) wide. Swift streams radiating down the mountains through lush forest and cropland to the sea cross both islands. At sea level, the climate is tropical --hot and humid with average yearly temperatures of about 27oC (80oF) and little daily variation. At the interior's higher altitudes, the average yearly temperature is 20oC (68oF), and nights are generally cool. Annual rainfall varies from 500 centimetres (200 in.) on the southwestern slopes to 100 centimetres (40 in.) in the northern lowlands. The rainy season runs from October to May. 2017.state.gov/outofdate/bgn/saotomeandprincipe/106168.htm

subsections.title: 2023 Report on International Religious Freedom
subsections.content:
Sao Tome and Principe

- The constitution and the law on religious freedom provide for freedom of

religion and worship and equality for all, irrespective of religious belief, and provide for judicial protection to all religious denominations.  Both the constitution and the religious freedom law grant religious groups autonomy and the right to teach their religion. Religious groups must register with the government. Registration requires at least 500 member signatures and Ministry of Justice approval

- Religious education is not a part of the official public -school curriculum. There

are two schools run by religious groups, one Catholic and one Seventh -day Adventist; both provide a general education and require all students to take religion classes and th e The Ministry of Education provides oversight on the curricula of religious schools.

- Article 8 from the General Constitutional Provisions enshrines the separation of

the state from religion.

subsections.title: The legal system in São Tomé and Príncipe
subsections.content:
- Formal legislation molded in diverse ways –namely as laws, law decrees, decrees,

regulations, regional decrees, and executive regional decrees –are the primary internal sources of law in São Tomé. Customary Laws also play a role in certain matters, mostly to explain or go beyond the plain meaning, but only if not in contradiction with the formal laws (secundum legis).

- It plays a crucial role in upholding the principles of  governance  and ensuring a

just society. As a fundamental framework, it is designed to maintain order, safeguard individual rights, and provide a mechanism for resolving disputes among individuals, organizations, and the state. The legal system is anchored in the cou ntry’s Constitution, which establishes the rule of  law as a cornerstone for democratic governance and civil rights.

- The Legal system is heavily influenced by Portuguese  law, due to its colonial

past, and incorporates other elements pertinent to the unique context of the islands. This blend of legal traditions creates a system that is both complex and adaptable, allowing for the evolution of legal norms in response to contempo rary societal needs.

- The legal framework in São Tomé and Príncipe comprises several court types,

each with defined functions and jurisdictions that form the backbone of the judiciary. The primary courts include the Constitutional Court, Administrative Court, and Ordinary Court s, each serving unique roles in the legal system. Diário da República of São Tomé and Príncipe (28 February 2025)

- It’s a Decree -Law (No. 02/2025)  that sets out the structure and organization of

the 19th Constitutional Government of São Tomé and Príncipe . In simple terms, it explains how the government is arranged, which ministries exist, ( as previously Stated in the Political Section) and what each one is responsible for. The Modern Legal Foundation for Investment Since 2016, São Tomé and Príncipe has fundamentally overhauled its investment framework, creating one of the more progressive legal structures in the region. Two cornerstone laws define the current environment: Investment Code (Decree -Law No. 19/2016)  establishes the terms, conditions, and guarantees for all investments in STP. Tax Benefits Code (Decree -Law No. 15/2016)  details the financial and fiscal incentives available to investors, defining exceptional measures that reduce or eliminate taxes to encourage economic development in priority sectors. Together, these laws create a clear regulatory foundation focused on attracting foreign capital while ensuring equal treatment between domestic and foreign investors guarantee enshrined in both legislation and the country's Constitution. The types of investment that are subject to the Investment Code are broadly defined. They should relate to economic activities that are developed by companies that are organized under the laws of São Tomé or that are registered within the jurisdiction. The investment framework operates on a tiered system based on project value, with different incentive levels corresponding to investment size: Minimum Threshold : To qualify for guarantees and tax incentives, investments must equal or exceed  €50,000 . This relatively low barrier makes STP accessible to small and medium -sized investors, not just major corporations.

subsections.title: Investments in Sao Tome and Principe
subsections.content:
Three Investment Regimes : 1. Simplified Regime  (€50,000 to €249,999): Projects receive 50% of the incentives described in the Tax Benefits Code 2. General Regime  (€250,000 to €4,999,999): Full access to standard incentives 3. Special Regime  (€5,000,000 or more): Maximum incentive package with negotiated terms To access these benefits, investors must enter into an Administrative Investment Contract (AIC) with the state. This contract requires several elements: investors must possess at least 20% of the proposed capital available, demonstrate stable financial standing, present clearance certificates showing no debts with the state or social security, and provide a feasibility study demonstrating job creation and social responsibility. Core Investment Guarantees The Investment Code provides fundamental protections that address investors' primary concerns:

- Equal Treatment : The law guarantees non -discriminatory treatment between

nationals and foreigners, regardless of capital origin. Importantly, there are no legal restrictions on foreign ownership of São Toméan companies —100% foreign ownership is permitted in most sectors.

- Expropriation Protection : The state guarantees that investment assets will not

be nationalized, expropriated, or requisitioned except for weighty public interest reasons. Even then, fair, prior, and effective compensation must be paid.

- Management Autonomy : Public non -interference in private enterprise

management is guaranteed, except in cases expressly provided by law.

- International Arbitration : STP is a signatory to the ICSID Convention

(Washington Convention of 1965) and the New York Convention on arbitration, providing independent dispute resolution mechanisms and reducing political risk. The Administrative Investment Contract (CAI): The CAI is a formal contract between you (the investor) and the State of São Tomé and Príncipe. Think of it as a bilateral agreement where both parties make binding commitments: You commit to:

- Investing a specific amount of capital

- Meeting implementation timelines

- Creating jobs and training local workers

- Achieving defined economic and social objectives

The government commits to:

- Granting specific tax incentives and benefits

- Protecting your investment against expropriation

- Allowing profit repatriation (subject to forex rules)

- Not interfering in your business management

This mutual commitment structure is what makes the CAI powerful. Unlike general laws that can be changed by parliament, your CAI is a  contract —it can only be altered by mutual agreement or if you violate its terms. Policies toward Foreign Direct Investment According to Article 4 of the Investment Code, both domestic and foreign investors are free to establish and own business enterprises, as well as engage in all forms of business activity in São Tomé and Príncipe, except in the sectors defined by law as reserved for the state, specifically military and paramilitary activities, and Central Bank operations. According to Article 6 of the Investment Code (Decree -Law No. 19/2016)  , it identifies some areas for investment.

- Both citizens and foreigners  can invest (while preserving and guarantying the

following

- Investor’s Protection against discrimination  (foreign and local investors are

treated equally).

- Investments will not be unfairly taken away (“expropriated”) without proper

compensation.

- Investments can be in areas like agriculture, tourism, energy, infrastructure, and

services.

- The government encourages projects that bring technology, training, and

innovation . Navigator | UNCTAD Investment Policy Hub

subsections.title: Land Access in Sao Tome and Principe
subsections.content:
Land access is often the most complex issue for foreign investors —and São Tomé and Príncipe is no exception After independence. The state became the dominant landowner & much of the country's productive land remains state -owned. The restriction : São Toméan law  prohibits foreign investors from possessing state lands . The general limit : Foreign nationals can own maximum  two hectares  of private land. Land access in São Tomé and Príncipe is possible through renewable concessions , but success depends less on paperwork and more on community engagement and careful due diligence . The legal rights are clear, but the “social license to operate” is what determines whether a project can move forward smoothly. Concession System

- Mechanism : Investors don’t own land outright; they receive 20-year

concessions , renewable automatically.

- Rights granted : Possession, use, and enjoyment of land; lease agreements;

exploitation rights.

- Termination : Either party can end with 2 years’ notice.

- Fees : Agricultural concessions cost about $10 –20 per hectare/year;

tourism/infrastructure fees are negotiated. Article 17. from the General Constitutional Provisions: Foreigners in São Tomé and Príncipe

- The exercise of public office only will be permitted to foreigners provided it has a

predominantly technical nature.

- Subject to reciprocal terms, the law may grant foreign citizens resident in the

national territory active and passive electoral capacity for the election of the holders of the organs of local government.

- Article 17 of the Constitution protects the rights and integrity of foreigners.

Foreigners and displaced persons who reside or stay in São Tomé and Príncipe enjoy the same rights and are subject to the same obligations as a São Tomean citizen, except insof ar as are concerned political rights, the exercise of public office, and other rights and obligations expressly reserved by law for the national citizen. Article 15. Principles of Equality

- All citizens are equal before the law, enjoy the same rights and are subject to the

same obligations

- Woman is equal to man in rights and obligations, being guaranteed to her full

participation in political, economic, social and cultural life.

subsections.title: Regulatory Authority for Supplying Medicines
subsections.content:
- The Central Supply of Medicines (Central de Aprovisionamento de

Medicamentos) (CAME) is an institution under the Ministry of Health to supply the Sao Tomean market with medicines and hospital consumables. The CAME in connection with the National Medicines F und (Fundo Nacional de Medicamentos) (FNM), a semi -autonomous governmental organization, is responsible for procuring, stocking and distributing essential medicines for the public sector on behalf of Ministry of Health (Ministry of Health of STP, n.d. -b).

- All medicines in Sao Tome and Principe are imported (Martinho do Rosário,

2008). As of 2007, drugs are procured through the International Dispensary Association (IDA). The IDA ensures quality, though prices are low (Martinho do Rosário, 2008).

subsections.title: Residence Visa
subsections.content:
For longer stays, this visa leads to residency and is categorized by purpose. It requires a valid travel document and, for minors, parental authorization. Applications are submitted at STP embassies or consulates, with processing up to 30 days.

- For Subordinate Professional Activity:  Submit an employment contract with

a favorable opinion from the Ministry of Labor (issued within 20 days), verifying contractual terms and lack of suitable local candidates. Foreign worker quotas apply (preference for locals).

- For Independent Professional Activity:  Prove foreign investment or sufficient

funds for self -employment, plus qualifications where needed.

- For Research or Highly Qualified Positions:  Affiliation with recognized

research centers, a job offer, and return guarantees if stay becomes irregular.

- For Study, Exchange, Internship, or Volunteer:  Valid travel document;

minors need parental consent.

- For Family Reunification:  SMF notifies the Ministry of Foreign Affairs for

immediate issuance post -approval. Authorizations and Procedures for Obtaining Residency Temporary Residence Certificate:Permanent Residence Certificate: Once in STP on a residence visa, apply for a residence certificate at the SMF office or through a legal representative. General conditions include a valid visa, police clearance, health certificate, and proof of accommodation/funds. Processing takes 15-30 days, with fees around STN 5,000 -10,000 ($220 -450). Temporary Residence Certificate: Valid  for one year from issuance, renewable annually or upon changes in details. Allows work/study as per visa. Permanent Residence Certificate: No expiry but renew every five years or on changes. Granted after several years of temporary residency, demonstrating integration (e.g., language, contributions). Exceptional Regimes Per a Government Decree from April 2017, citizens of certain countries (e.g., EU, USA, Canada) enjoy visa -free entry for up to 15 days for tourism/business. US citizens can stay up to 30 days visa -free. Chinese holders of diplomatic/special passports get 1 5 days exemption, following diplomatic reestablishment. Recent visa waivers (ratified 2025) with Ghana, Mozambique, Colombia, and Dominica allow reciprocal 15 -day stays, enhancing regional ties. Extensions are possible via SMF for justified reasons. SaoTomeExpert

subsections.title: Religious Freedom Laws
subsections.content:
### 2.6.6.1 — Constitutional Guarantees The Constitution of the Democratic Republic of São Tomé and Príncipe, in its most recent revision of 2003, provides robust guarantees of religious freedom. Article 27 explicitly declares that freedom of conscience, religion, and worship is inviolable speci fying that no citizen may be persecuted, deprived of rights, or exempted from civic duties on account of religious conviction or practice. Article 8 establishes São Tomé and Príncipe as a secular (lay) state, stipulating a clear separation between state institutions and all religious institutions. Article 265 criminalizes 'religious coercion', defined as compelling a person to participate or abstain from religious worship, and provides for up to six months' imprisonment for violations.

- Constitute Project. Constitution of São Tomé and Príncipe (2003).

- Freedom of Thought Report: São Tomé and Príncipe. Op. cit. Humanists

International . ### 2.6.6.2 — Religious Registration Process Religious groups must register with the government of São Tomé and Príncipe; however, the process is not onerous or discriminatory. The U.S. State Department's 2019 and 2020 Religious Freedom Reports confirm that no group has ever been denied registration,  and no unregistered group has been restricted from operation. The registration procedure requires:

- Submission of a written letter requesting authorization from the Ministry of

Justice and Human Rights.

- Submission of the group's statutes and meeting minutes to a notary public,

signed by the president and secretary.

- Certification from the Registrar's Office that no existing organization bears

the same name.

- Payment of notarial fees (historically approximately USD 45 –50).

- Publication of approval in the official government gazette.

Once registered, a religious group enjoys the same tax -exempt status as registered nonprofit organizations and need not re -register. Foreign religious groups that fail to register are subject to fines and possible expulsion, making timely registration a priority for the Coptic mission team. U.S. Department of State. 2019 Report on International Religious Freedom: São Tomé and Príncipe .
